opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny — it's changed quite a bit. When I was in grad school, I was actually somewhat skeptical of working on language. My training was much more on the machine learning side: statistical learning theory, probabilistic models, things like that. And language, at the time, felt like this messy domain with a lot of hand-engineered features and pipelines, where it was hard to say something clean or principled. I think I sort of consciously steered away from it. I gravitated toward problems where I felt like the math could carry you, and language didn't quite feel like that.

What changed, honestly, is that the field changed underneath me. Once large language models started working the way they do now, language stopped being just one application area among many and became kind of the interface to everything. A lot of the questions I've cared about for a long time — how do you evaluate a model properly, what does it mean for a metric to reflect what you actually want, how do you think about fairness and robustness and reliability — suddenly became really central questions for language models. So it wasn't so much that I decided to become a language person; it's that the core problems I was already working on started showing up most urgently in language.

And I've come to really appreciate that the messiness I was nervous about is actually where a lot of the interesting science is. Things like measurement — you know, when we say a model has some capability, or that some ability "emerges" at scale, how much of that is about the model and how much is about the metric we chose? Those are questions where the statistical and theoretical tools I was trained in turn out to be genuinely useful. So I'd say I went from kind of avoiding language to finding it one of the most exciting places to apply that more principled lens.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language felt messy, reliant on hand-engineered features and pipelines, and difficult to approach cleanly or principledly. It does not identify difficulty understanding field-specific jargon as a reason for avoiding language research.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. It's funny, because when I was in graduate school I was pretty deliberately not a language person. My training was in machine learning more broadly, and a lot of my early work was on the statistical side, on things like metrics, evaluation, and the theory of how you measure whether a model is actually doing what you want. Language felt like a specialized subfield with its own community and its own conventions, and honestly I thought of it as somebody else's problem.

What changed is that language models stopped being a subfield and became the substrate for almost everything. Once the same model is being used for coding, for medical question answering, for tutoring, for decision support, the questions I had always cared about, like how do you know this thing is trustworthy, how do you evaluate it fairly, how do you reason about its failure modes, suddenly land squarely on language systems. So in some sense I didn't move toward language research so much as language research moved toward the problems I was already obsessed with.

The other shift is in how I think about rigor. In grad school, the aesthetic was that a good result came with a clean theorem and a tidy benchmark. With modern language models, a lot of the most important questions don't yet have that shape. We're often working with systems we didn't train, can't fully inspect, and that behave very differently depending on how you prompt them. Early on I found that frustrating. Now I see it as a scientific opportunity. My group spends a lot of energy on evaluation, on figuring out what a benchmark score actually means, on whether a reported gain is real or an artifact of how the test was constructed. That's a very different attitude from the one I had as a student, where I would have wanted the measurement problem solved before I was willing to engage.

And I'd say the stakes feel different too. These systems are in people's lives now. That makes me more patient with messy, empirical, sometimes unglamorous work, because getting the measurement right is how we keep the field honest.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language felt like a specialized subfield with its own community and conventions, but does not identify difficulty understanding its jargon as a reason for avoiding language research.

astra-6.text:
I’ve become much more interested in it. In graduate school, I tended to stay away from language because it felt messy and difficult to pin down. I was more comfortable with problems where you could make the assumptions explicit and reason carefully about what a method should do.

Now, that messiness is part of what makes language interesting to me. These systems raise questions about how we evaluate models, what it means for them to be reliable, and whether the things we measure actually capture what people care about. So I’ve gone from seeing language as something I’d rather avoid to seeing it as a place where a lot of the questions I care about come together.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language felt messy and difficult to pin down, but does not identify difficulty understanding field-specific jargon as a reason for avoiding it.

sol-6.1.text: In graduate school, I was pretty reluctant to work on language. It seemed like you needed a lot of domain knowledge just to understand which problems were interesting, and I was more drawn to general machine learning questions. That’s changed quite a bit. Language models have become a really useful setting for studying questions I care about, particularly around evaluation, reliability, and how we make these systems behave the way we want. So I’ve gone from thinking, “That’s probably somebody else’s area,” to seeing a lot of opportunities to contribute.
